name: Yara Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or the government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes back to your employer with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the primary crusher and the conveyors at a big lithium mine. The trucks tip the rock into the crusher, and I keep it fed without choking it, watch the belts, clear blockages, and talk to the plant control room all day on the radio. Half my day's out on the walkways with a torch and half's in the little crusher hut looking at screens. I like solving problems, like when a belt's tracking off and you have to work out why, and what wears me out is the noise, even with earmuffs, you go home with a hum in your head.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use AI tools every day. How?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I've got one on my phone and I use it for everything. At work, after a shift I'll describe a weird fault and ask it what might cause it, and about half the time it points me somewhere useful. At home I use it to plan meals for the week and to help Isla with her reading. Rafa, my partner, runs a little landscaping business and I've set him up with it for his quotes, he grumbled at first but now he won't give it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a handy tool, just not the miracle people promised. I use it every day, so I'd defend it a bit. At work I'd say, see, it didn't take your job, it just helps you find a fault faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, maybe slightly disappointing. I like the stuff, I'd have liked to see what it could really do. But my job's safe enough and the pay's good, so I'm not complaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it for faults and paperwork and try to get the site to let us use it officially, right now we're all just doing it on our phones. I'd keep putting a bit into an index fund, about a hundred a fortnight, like I've been doing. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd want the site to let you use it officially. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A version that knows our actual crusher, the manuals, the fault history. Right now I'm typing it all in by hand from memory. If it had our records, it'd be twice as good, and I'd happily help set that up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned an index fund. Is that unusual among your workmates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Most of the guys have their money in the house and the boat. I started three years ago after watching videos on it, it's only about six thousand dollars, but it's mine. My dad thinks it's gambling.

S0.say: I'd say AI is still a handy tool, just not the promised miracle. At work I'd point out it didn't take anyone's job, it just helps find faults faster.
S0.think: It's fine for me and maybe slightly disappointing, because I'd have liked to see what it could do. My job is safe enough and the pay is good.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for faults and paperwork and pushes the site to adopt it officially with its own records. Keeps putting about a hundred a fortnight into an index fund.
S0.feel: Calm, and a tiny bit bored.
S0.quote: Right now I'm typing it all in by hand from memory.
S0.fieldNote: Yara is the rare worker who'd be a little disappointed by the plateau. She already pushes AI into her work informally and would help the site formalise it. Her small index fund marks her as someone who takes measured risks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so let's get good at it. At work I'd tell the younger ones to get in early, volunteer for the trials. I'd also say the company should be fair about it, but I wouldn't be on a soapbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is good for me. Crushers and conveyors are going to get automated controls, and someone has to run the system and fix it when it goes wrong. I'd want to be that person, and I think I've got a decent shot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down this month for any trial of automated crusher control. I'd ask the company to pay for a course in plant control systems, it's about a year part time. I'd keep the index fund going and maybe bump it to one fifty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like the first day on a new site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary, on the secondary crusher. He's sixty and he's done it the same way for thirty years, and he's brilliant at it, he can hear a bad bearing from across the plant. But he won't touch a tablet. I'd try to pair up with him, I learn the sounds from him and he learns the screens from me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd volunteer for trials. What if the trial makes your own job disappear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd rather be the one who knows how the new thing works than the one it happens to. That's how I see it. Someone's going to run the trial, might as well be me.

S1.say: I'd say it's here, so let's get good at it, and tell younger workers to volunteer for trials. The company should be fair, but I wouldn't get on a soapbox.
S1.think: This is good for me, because crushers and conveyors will get automated controls and someone has to run and fix them. I think I've got a decent shot at being that person.
S1.do: Signs up this month for any trial of automated crusher control and asks the company to fund a year-long part-time plant control course. Raises her index fund contributions to about one fifty a fortnight.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like the first day on a new site.
S1.quote: Then I'd rather be the one who knows how the new thing works than the one it happens to.
S1.fieldNote: Yara openly sees steady change as an opportunity and would help bring automation into her own work. Her pragmatism shows in pairing with an older colleague rather than writing him off. She doesn't blame anyone; she just moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is huge and we need to be realistic, because pretending it isn't happening won't help anyone. I'd say the government and companies need to agree some way of sharing the gains fast. I wouldn't panic in public, people look to you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my plan of running the automated system lasts maybe a year, and then the AI runs the system. Being early buys me time, not safety. That's the bit that stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grab every hour of overtime in the first year and push savings from about four months to as much as I could. I'd try to get a job with the company installing the new systems, they'd need people who know the site, even if it's only for a year or two. And I'd move some of the index fund into shares in the companies making the robots, a small amount, because if they're taking the work, I'd like a slice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited and scared at the same time, which is a strange mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only having two years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd be early to a party that ends at nine. In a slower version, being early gives you a career. In this one it gives you maybe eighteen months before you're in the same boat as everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put money into robot companies. How would that feel, given it's your own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit grim, I'll admit. Rafa would say I'm betting against myself. But it's only a couple of thousand, it's not going to save us, it's more like, if the world goes that way, I'm not completely on the wrong side of it.

S2.say: I'd say this is huge and we need to be realistic about it. Government and companies need to agree on sharing the gains quickly, and I wouldn't panic in public.
S2.think: My plan of running the automated system lasts maybe a year before the AI runs it. Being early buys me time, not safety, and that stings.
S2.do: Takes every overtime shift to build savings beyond about four months and seeks work installing the new systems for a year or two. Moves a couple of thousand dollars of her index fund into shares in robot makers.
S2.feel: Anxious, excited and scared at the same time.
S2.quote: It means I'd be early to a party that ends at nine.
S2.fieldNote: Yara sees clearly that being early only buys time in the fast picture. She stays anxious rather than alarmed because she has a concrete short-term path and savings. Her small bet on robot makers shows both her pragmatism and her discomfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but workable, so everyone should start now. At work I'd say, don't wait for the company, go and learn something. I'd tell people about the free online courses I'd found.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me one good move and a bit of a buffer. I could get into installing and commissioning the automated systems, that's setting them up and getting them running, and do it at other mines too. After that I honestly don't know, but I'd have money put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the plant control course this year and apply to the companies that install these systems, even if it means some travel. I'd keep the index fund going and get the savings to six months. And I'd help Rafa get a robot mower or two for his landscaping, so his business grows instead of getting replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly busy. I'm better when I've got a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Travel would be hard with young kids. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Isla's nine and Leo's six, so it would be tough. Rafa's hours are flexible, so he'd take more of the school runs, and my mum's ten minutes away. I'd cap it at a year, two weeks away a month, and we'd see how the kids handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy robots for Rafa's business. How does he feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He thinks it's cheating. He loves mowing, he says it's thinking time. But he's also got a sore back and two kids, so he'd come round, especially if it meant he could take on the bigger council contracts.

S3.say: I'd say five years is tight but workable, so everyone should start now. I'd tell workmates not to wait for the company and point them to free online courses.
S3.think: Five years gives me one good move and a buffer, installing and commissioning automated systems at different mines. After that I honestly don't know, but I'd have savings.
S3.do: Finishes the plant control course this year and applies to system installers, accepting up to a year of travel. Builds savings to six months and helps her partner buy robot mowers for his landscaping business.
S3.feel: Uneasy but mostly busy, better with a list.
S3.quote: He loves mowing, he says it's thinking time.
S3.fieldNote: Yara turns the five-year window into a sequence of practical steps and family logistics. She'd bring automation into her partner's business too, which he resists on principle. Her lack of blame and calm planning mark her centre outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get ready, so there's no excuse not to. I'd say it at work and at the school gate. I'd probably start a group chat for people at the mine who want to learn together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is good. I'd ride the automation wave for six or seven years, and with the index fund and some savings I'd have some choices by fifty-three. What worries me more is what Isla and Leo will do, because they'd be teenagers in a world where nobody knows what a job is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the plant control course and then maybe a diploma in automation over a few years. I'd keep investing, maybe a bit more each year as pay goes up. And Rafa and I would start setting aside a little for the kids' education, whatever that looks like by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, in a low way. More curious than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been fairly calm throughout. What's the thing you'd lose sleep over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the money from all this goes to a handful of people. Then my little index fund wouldn't matter much and nobody's job would. I don't usually get political, but I'd vote for whoever had a real plan for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Isla about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn to do lots of different things and not get attached to one job. And to keep reading, because she struggles with it and I worry. Whatever the world looks like, people who can read and think will be better off.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to get ready, so there's no excuse. I'd start a group chat for workmates who want to learn together.
S4.think: Ten years is good for me: six or seven years riding automation, then savings and investments to give me choices. I worry more about what my kids will do.
S4.do: Does the plant control course and then an automation diploma over a few years. Keeps investing more as pay rises and starts saving for the children's education.
S4.feel: Uneasy in a low way, more curious than scared.
S4.quote: I don't usually get political, but I'd vote for whoever had a real plan for that.
S4.fieldNote: Yara stays in the calm-to-uneasy range across most pictures, which follows from her early adoption and savings habit. Her deeper worry is the money from automation going to a few people, which pulls her toward politics for the first time. She thinks in long sequences of steps.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: We've been through all five pictures. Of the five, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because being early wouldn't save me. What would help is good, quick courses for real jobs, and some way of everyone getting a share of what the robots earn, not just the shareholders. And straight information, I can handle bad news if it's honest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they're already doing. Half the guys on my crew are using AI on their phones and not telling anyone, because they think they'll get in trouble. The change is already happening quietly.

headlineQuote: Half the guys on my crew are using AI on their phones and not telling anyone, because they think they'll get in trouble.
portrait: Yara Lopez is a 43-year-old crusher and conveyor operator at a large lithium mine, with a partner who runs a small landscaping business, two young kids and a small index fund she started on her own. She uses AI every day and would volunteer for automation trials, believing it's better to understand a change than to have it happen to you. She stays calm in the milder pictures and anxious at worst, because she sees concrete next steps, though she admits that in the two-year picture being early only buys time. Her deeper worry is that the gains go to a few people, which is the one thing that would pull her into politics.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because being early to automation would only buy her about eighteen months.
whatWouldHelp: Good quick courses for real jobs, a fair share of what robots earn going to everyone, and honest information.
